attrs.label: Method + path
attrs.plain: The endpoint's name — the verb and the URL a client calls.
attrs.eg: POST /setup/complete

attrs.label: Entity · cluster
attrs.plain: The feature that owns the endpoint and the URL group it sits in.
attrs.eg: entity auth · URL group setup

attrs.label: Declared status
attrs.plain: The success code the endpoint promises in its decorator.
attrs.eg: 200, the framework default · no refusal is declared

attrs.label: File:line
attrs.plain: The file and line where the handler starts.
attrs.eg: apps/api/api/setup.py:183

attrs.label: Risk flag
attrs.plain: A warning that the endpoint is unusually large or heavily used.
attrs.eg: flagged large surface · 29 functions sit behind the handler

attrs.label: Signature (async · lines · returns)
attrs.plain: The handler's outline — async or not, its length, the type it returns.
attrs.eg: async · 21 lines · returns MeResponse

attrs.label: Usage · fan-in
attrs.plain: The number of callers that reach the endpoint.
attrs.eg: fan-in 1 · 1 caller from the API side, 0 internal

attrs.label: Kinds of ending (success · refusal · framework · validation · uncaught)
attrs.plain: The families a request's ending can belong to — success, refusal, framework, validation, uncaught.
attrs.eg: success 3 · refusal 7 · framework 2 · validation 1 · uncaught 1

attrs.label: The endings (paths)
attrs.plain: Every distinct way a request to the endpoint can end.
attrs.eg: 14 endings · among them “Idempotency-Key required”, “setup in progress”, “consent required”, “replay” and 10 more

attrs.label: The stage an ending leaves from
attrs.plain: The stage where a request stops — edge, gate, input, handler, answer or uncaught.
attrs.eg: EDGE 2 · GATE 2 · INPUT 3 · HANDLER 3 · ANSWER 3 · UNCAUGHT 1

attrs.label: Status code per ending
attrs.plain: The HTTP number each ending answers with.

attrs.label: Own guards (preconditions)
attrs.plain: A check in the handler's own code that refuses the request.
attrs.eg: 3 guards · “key is None” ends 400

attrs.label: Deciding branches (callee arms that change the exit)
attrs.plain: A branch inside a called function that changes how the request ends.
attrs.eg: 3 branches inside complete_setup · REPLAY · completed · fall-through

attrs.label: Catches (translate · swallow · pass through)
attrs.plain: A try/except that turns a failure into a status — or hides the failure.
attrs.eg: 5 catches · SetupInProgressError becomes a 409

attrs.label: Switches (binding · value · flag)
attrs.plain: A setting or a swapped-in implementation that changes what the endpoint does.
attrs.eg: 3 switches · binding TokenVerifier · value ai_credits_chef · flag environment + rate_limit_enabled

attrs.label: Steps in the longest chain
attrs.plain: The count of steps on the longest way through the endpoint.
attrs.eg: 22 steps on “first run” (200)

attrs.label: Tables touched
attrs.plain: The database tables the endpoint reads or writes.
attrs.eg: 15 tables across all endings · the Data panel draws 13 of them

attrs.label: Operation per table (read · write · both; add · update · delete)
attrs.plain: The kind of touch each table gets — read, add, update or delete.
attrs.eg: read only: consent_records, ai_spend_log · written: 13 tables

attrs.label: Fate of the writes per ending (committed · maybe · rolled back · uncommitted)
attrs.plain: The outcome of the writes on one ending — saved, rolled back or left unsaved.
attrs.eg: on “consent required” (409) · 1 committed · 9 rolled back · 1 maybe committed

attrs.label: The moment a table is touched (stage · step)
attrs.plain: The stage and step at which a table is touched.
attrs.eg: users is read first, in resolve_or_create_user, at the GATE before the handler runs

attrs.label: Provisions (rows created before the handler)
attrs.plain: A row the endpoint creates before the handler even starts.
attrs.eg: a users row is added at the gate and committed

attrs.label: Race on a unique key
attrs.plain: Two simultaneous requests that insert the same unique key.
attrs.eg: 11 uncaught races · on users, locations and 9 more · idempotency_keys is handled

attrs.label: Idempotency claim
attrs.plain: A key that makes a request safe to send twice.
attrs.eg: Idempotency-Key header · required, a missing key ends 400

attrs.label: Events published (the event · the handlers subscribed to it)
attrs.plain: An event the endpoint announces, and the other code that runs because it heard it.
attrs.eg: none on this endpoint

attrs.label: Tasks dispatched (background work that outlives the answer)
attrs.plain: Background work the endpoint starts that keeps running after the answer.
attrs.eg: none on this endpoint

attrs.label: Outside services called (an LLM, an identity provider, a payment API)
attrs.plain: A service outside the app the endpoint calls — an LLM, an identity provider, a payment API.
attrs.eg: none drawn on this endpoint

attrs.label: Request-scoped state (a key set by middleware, the auth context)
attrs.plain: A value set early in the request that later steps rely on — the auth context, a key on request.state.
attrs.eg: request.state.idempotency_key is set by middleware and read by the handler

attrs.label: Client cache effects (keys invalidated · seeded)
attrs.plain: The cached queries the screen drops or refills after the answer.
attrs.eg: on success · seeds “me” · invalidates “me”, “settings”

attrs.label: Request shape
attrs.plain: The schema the request body must match.
attrs.eg: SetupCompleteRequest · 7 fields

attrs.label: Response shape per ending
attrs.plain: The body each ending answers with.
attrs.eg: MeResponse with 6 fields on the 200 · 10 other endings answer with a detail

attrs.label: Delivery (one answer · a stream)
attrs.plain: The way the answer travels — one reply, or a stream that keeps sending.
attrs.eg: one answer · no stream

attrs.label: Validation cases (the 422 rules)
attrs.plain: The rules that make a request body fail with a 422.
attrs.eg: 2 tests prove a 422 · C1051, C1052 · the rules themselves are not in the lab's facts yet
attrs.gap: not in the lab's facts yet

attrs.label: The handler (API-facing)
attrs.plain: The function that faces the API and receives the request.
attrs.eg: setup_complete · async, 21 lines, returns MeResponse

attrs.label: Decision-point functions (their raise or refusal becomes an ending)
attrs.plain: A function whose raise or refusal becomes one of the endings.
attrs.eg: complete_setup · 3 of its branches change the ending (REPLAY · completed · fall-through)

attrs.label: Data-touching functions (commit · read · write)
attrs.plain: A function that reads, writes or commits to the database.
attrs.eg: 23 functions touch the database · among them resolve_or_create_user, build_auth_context, load_household_context and 20 more

attrs.label: Context-giving functions (authentication · session · settings)
attrs.plain: A function that prepares context for the rest — authentication, the session, settings.
attrs.eg: get_auth_context · runs at the gate, before the handler

attrs.label: Little helpers, with a TYPE (format · cap · validate…)
attrs.plain: A small function that formats, caps or validates one value.
attrs.eg: none to show · helper functions carry no type in the feed yet
attrs.gap: the type is not classified today

attrs.label: Functions behind · walk levels
attrs.plain: The count of functions reachable behind the handler and the depth of that walk.
attrs.eg: 29 functions behind the handler · the call walk reaches 27, 4 levels deep (3 · 16 · 7 · 1)

attrs.label: Coverage per condition (covered · partial · untested · unmeasured)
attrs.plain: The share of endings and guards that a test proves.
attrs.eg: 7 of 14 endings have a test · none on “rate limit (sensitive)”, “rate limit (global)”, “json_invalid (framework)” and 4 more

attrs.label: Cases (C-ids)
attrs.plain: The named test cases that prove an ending.
attrs.eg: 26 cases · 26 pass

attrs.label: Journeys · workflow step
attrs.plain: The user journey the endpoint is one step of.
attrs.eg: step 2 of 4 in “Initial setup — first run”

attrs.label: Auth scheme + gate
attrs.plain: The login scheme and the function that checks it.
attrs.eg: HTTPBearer on the Authorization header · checked by get_auth_context

attrs.label: Rate limit
attrs.plain: The cap on the requests one client may send per minute.
attrs.eg: 20 per 60 s (sensitive) · 120 per 60 s (global)

attrs.label: App band (middleware)
attrs.plain: The middleware every request in the app passes through.
attrs.eg: 3 middleware · the same on all 80 endpoints

attrs.label: Who fetches it (hook → screen)
attrs.plain: The frontend hook that calls the endpoint and the screen that uses the hook.
attrs.eg: useCompleteSetup → HouseholdStep, SetupContent, SetupStateTabs

attrs.label: Can the client tell the endings apart
attrs.plain: The screen's ability to tell two different refusals apart.
attrs.eg: two 409s, “consent required” and “setup in progress”, reach one branch in SetupScreen.tsx

attrs.label: Findings
attrs.plain: The anomalies the form check found on the endpoint.
attrs.eg: 4 findings · 5 refusals told apart only by the message · two refusals share the 409 · undeclared statuses 400, 401, 409, 429 · a refusal that still writes

questions.text: At which moment is a table touched, and on what does that depend?
On THIS ending, which tables were written, and did the write survive?
Which endings can this door produce, and at which stage does each one leave?
Which conditions of this door does a test prove, and which does nothing reach?
What should be at this stage for this topic?
Which gate stopped this request, and which ones did it pass first?
What executes after what inside the door?
What does the client do with each ending — can it tell two 409s apart?
Which tables does the door touch that the Data panel never draws?
What fields does this entity carry, and how do they hang together?
Which route is the expected one, and which are the exceptions?
Is this door built from standard pieces, or did it go specialist?
What shape goes in and what shape comes back on this ending?
Which door is the densest, the riskiest, the least tested?
Where in the code is this — can I open it?
What did the door save temporarily — cache, or something ephemeral that was alive and important during the process?
What determines the path — what makes this a 401, a 402 or a 200?
Which functions are the crucial ones: facing the API, deciding the ending, touching the database, giving context?
Which little functions sit inside the loop, and of what type (formatting · capping · validation…)?
What is inside this element, and what is there to explore — implications, effects, impact, coverage?
